statement: Amortized chrono::steady_clock wall-time guard (every 512 B&B nodes at 700ms) with fast I/O (fread/printf) improves Docker judge reliability from 70% to 80% at score 100 (mean 98.5 -> 99.0) compared to clock()-based CPU-time guard, but cannot eliminate the ~20% residual failure rate caused by irreducible Docker container overhead.
regime: B&B solver running in Docker with 1s time limit; algorithm completes in <25ms locally; Docker overhead 3-5x
mechanism: chrono::steady_clock measures wall time (not CPU time like clock()), directly matching Docker's 1s wall-time limit. Amortizing checks to every 512 nodes (bnb_nodes & 511 == 0) eliminates the ~100% overhead of per-node chrono calls. Fast I/O (fread/printf/char[]) avoids string/stream heap allocations. Together these keep total wall time under 100ms locally. However, Docker container startup + CPU scheduling overhead occasionally exceeds 300ms (out of 1s budget), causing TLEs regardless of algorithm speed.
applicability_bounds: Applies when the bottleneck is Docker wall-time overhead rather than algorithm computation time. When algorithm time dominates (>500ms locally), the guard threshold and amortization period need adjustment.

statement: Docker timing variability causes 5% score drops (95 instead of 100) in the B&B solver on ~20% of judge runs. Wall-time guards (chrono::steady_clock) are necessary but not sufficient — the ~20% failure rate from Docker container overhead is likely irreducible by algorithmic optimization alone.
regime: B&B solver with 1s Docker time limit, algorithm <25ms locally
mechanism: Docker container startup, CPU scheduling, and I/O overhead occasionally consume 300-500ms of the 1s budget. A clock()-based guard (CPU time) missed this because Docker overhead is wall-time-only. A chrono::steady_clock guard reduces but cannot eliminate the issue.
applicability_bounds: Docker containers with 1s time limits and sub-100ms algorithms
